clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive salt-losing tubulopathy caused by loss-of-function variants in SLC12A3, which encodes the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule
The biochemical signature is hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with hypomagnesaemia and, characteristically, low urinary calcium excretion (hypocalciuria)
It effectively mimics the biochemical effect of chronic thiazide diuretic use, so surreptitious diuretic misuse must be excluded
Presentation is often in adolescence or adulthood with fatigue, muscle cramps and weakness, tetany, carpopedal spasm and salt craving, and it is generally milder than Bartter syndrome
Blood pressure tends to be low or low-normal and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is activated
The combination of hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria helps distinguish it from Bartter syndrome, which typically shows normal or high urinary calcium
Chondrocalcinosis and QT prolongation can complicate longstanding electrolyte disturbance
reference.pathophysiology: Gitelman-spectrum tubulopathy results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in SLC12A3, which encodes the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCCT) in the apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule. Impaired sodium and chloride reabsorption at this site causes mild renal salt wasting and volume contraction, which activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; the resulting increased distal sodium delivery and aldosterone drive potassium and hydrogen secretion, producing hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Associated downregulation and remodelling of the distal tubule impair magnesium reabsorption and enhance passive calcium reabsorption, generating the characteristic hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria. The phenotype thus recapitulates chronic thiazide exposure.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of hypomagnesaemia (e.g. drug-induced, gastrointestinal loss)
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes including potassium, magnesium, bicarbonate and calcium
Blood gas or bicarbonate to confirm metabolic alkalosis
Urinary electrolytes and, where needed, a urinary diuretic screen to exclude surreptitious diuretic use
Plasma renin and aldosterone showing activation of the axis
Genetic testing of SLC12A3 (and related tubulopathy genes) to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: Severe hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia with cardiac arrhythmia or marked QT prolongation
Tetany or seizures from profound electrolyte depletion
Acute decompensation during intercurrent illness with vomiting or diarrhoea
reference.prognosis: Gitelman syndrome generally has a good long-term prognosis with appropriate electrolyte supplementation and normal life expectancy in most patients, although chronic symptoms and occasional severe electrolyte disturbances can affect quality of life. Kidney function is usually preserved.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude surreptitious diuretic use, which produces an identical biochemical picture
Confusing it with Bartter syndrome by not checking urinary calcium and magnesium
Neglecting magnesium repletion, without which potassium is difficult to correct
Underestimating arrhythmia risk from combined hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia
management: Lifelong oral magnesium replacement as the cornerstone, since restoring magnesium is usually essential to correcting the hypokalaemia
Oral potassium supplementation alongside a liberal salt and fluid intake to compensate for renal salt wasting
Potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone, eplerenone or amiloride to limit renal potassium and magnesium wasting
Intravenous magnesium and potassium replacement for severe symptomatic depletion presenting with tetany, carpopedal spasm or arrhythmia
Periodic monitoring of serum electrolytes, with ECG when disturbance is marked, and counselling on salt and fluid maintenance during intercurrent illness
Confirm with SLC12A3 genetic testing and provide counselling for this autosomal recessive tubulopathy, screening at-risk siblings
